title: fmt & Formatted I/O
summary: The **fmt** package is Go's standard library for formatted input and output. It provides `Print`/`Println`/`Printf` for output, `Sprintf` for building strings, and verbs like `%d`, `%s`, `%v`, and `%+v` to control formatting. Implementing the `Stringer` interface customizes how your own types print.

subtopics.title: Print, Println, Printf
subtopics.explanation: Print writes its arguments with no separator; Println adds spaces between operands and a trailing newline; Printf uses a format string with verbs. Println is for quick output; Printf is for controlled formatting. These three functions are the core of fmt's formatted output.

subtopics.title: Sprintf builds strings
subtopics.explanation: The S-prefixed functions (Sprint, Sprintf) return a formatted string instead of printing it. Sprintf is the idiomatic way to build a formatted string from values. It brings fmt's verb-based formatting to string building, not just console output.

subtopics.title: Core format verbs
subtopics.explanation: %d formats integers, %s strings, %t booleans, %f floats, %q quoted strings, %x hex, and %v the value in a default format. Width/precision modifiers like %.2f and %5d control alignment and decimals. Knowing the core verbs is what lets fmt render each value the way you want.

subtopics.title: %v, %+v, %#v
subtopics.explanation: %v prints a value's default representation; %+v adds struct field names; %#v prints Go-syntax (the literal you'd type). These are invaluable for debugging structs. They are the fmt verbs you reach for most when inspecting values during development.

subtopics.title: Stringer and Fprintf
subtopics.explanation: Implement String() string (the fmt.Stringer interface) to control how %v/%s prints your type. Fprintf writes formatted output to any io.Writer (a file, network connection, or buffer), which is how you target destinations other than stdout. Together they show how fmt's formatting extends to custom types and arbitrary destinations.

foundations.overview: fmt is the package you reach for to print to the console, build formatted strings, and read simple input. It centers on a family of functions (Print, Printf, Sprintf, Fprintf) and a set of format verbs that describe how each value should be rendered. Knowing the common verbs and the Stringer interface lets you produce clean output and readable debug logs, and Fprintf generalizes printing to any destination.
foundations.formalDefinition: fmt is the standard package implementing formatted I/O with functions analogous to C's printf/scanf. Output functions take a format string with verbs (e.g., %d, %s, %v) and operands; the Stringer interface (String() string) lets types define their own textual form.
foundations.whyItMatters: Formatted output is how you debug, log, and build human-readable messages. Picking the right verb and implementing Stringer makes logs clear, and Fprintf to an io.Writer is the foundation of writing to files, responses, and buffers.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a format string as a fill-in-the-blank template: each verb is a labeled blank that says what kind of value goes there and how to dress it (width, precision, quoting). fmt walks the template and the operands together, filling blanks in order.
commonUseCases: Implementing Stringer for readable type output
Writing formatted output to files/responses via Fprintf

commonMisconceptions.myth: Println and Printf behave the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Println adds spaces between operands and a trailing newline; Printf prints exactly what the format string says — you add \n yourself.
%+v shows struct field names and %#v shows Go syntax — far more useful for debugging structs than bare %v.

commonMisconceptions.myth: fmt is the fastest way to format numbers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It uses reflection; strconv.Itoa/FormatFloat are faster in hot paths where you format the same simple type repeatedly.

visualExplorer.title: How Printf matches verbs to operands
visualExplorer.caption: fmt scans the format string left to right, consuming one operand per verb and formatting it by type.

steps.name: Find the first verb
steps.detail: %s consumes the first operand "cpu" and formats it as a string.

steps.name: Literal text passes through
steps.detail: ' is ' is not a verb, so it is copied to the output unchanged.

steps.name: Integer verb
steps.detail: %d consumes 80 and formats it as a decimal integer.

steps.name: Float with precision
steps.detail: %.1f consumes 80.0 and formats it with one decimal place: 80.0.

steps.name: Escaped percent
steps.detail: %% emits a literal '%'. The trailing \n adds a newline; result: 'cpu is 80 (80.0%)'.

interactiveExamples.title: Println vs Printf vs Sprintf
interactiveExamples.explanation: Println spaces operands and adds a newline. Printf follows the format string exactly (you add \n). Sprintf returns the string instead of printing it.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	name, age := "Ann", 30
	fmt.Println(name, age)                 // Ann 30
	fmt.Printf("%s is %d\n", name, age)   // Ann is 30
	s := fmt.Sprintf("%s(%d)", name, age)  // build a string
	fmt.Println(s)                          // Ann(30)
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the type print nicely with Stringer
interactiveExamples.explanation: By default %v prints a struct's fields. Implement String() string so Point prints as (x, y). Edit the code to add the method, then %v will use it.

checkpoints.explanation: %d prints 5, %s prints hi, and %.2f rounds 3.14159 to two decimals (3.14). The literal spaces in the format string separate them, and \n ends the line.

checkpoints.prompt: You want to debug a struct and SEE its field names. Which verb?
checkpoints.code:
type User struct{ ID int; Name string }
u := User{1, "Ann"}
checkpoints.explanation: %+v prints struct field names alongside values: {ID:1 Name:Ann}. Plain %v omits the names ({1 Ann}); %d and %s are wrong types for a struct.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this output show '%!d(string=hi)' instead of the value?
options: The verb %d expects an integer but got a string, so fmt reports a format error
checkpoints.explanation: %d is the integer verb, but the operand is a string, so fmt emits a bad-verb error: %!d(string=hi). Use %s for strings (or %v for any type).

checkpoints.prompt: Build a string 'id=42' without printing it.
checkpoints.explanation: Sprintf RETURNS the formatted string instead of writing it to stdout. Printf/Print/Println write directly and return counts/error, not the string.

codeLab.title: Format a price as currency
codeLab.instructions: Implement `FormatPrice(cents int) string` that returns a dollar string like "$12.05" from an integer number of cents. Use fmt verbs and integer math; do not use floating point (to avoid rounding errors).
hints: Use integer division and modulo to split cents into dollars and remainder.
%02d zero-pads to two digits so 5 cents shows as 05.
Avoid float math; it introduces rounding errors for money.

debuggingLab.title: Printf output runs together on one line
debuggingLab.symptom: Three Printf calls in a loop print everything on a single line.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Unlike Println, Printf does not add a trailing newline — it prints exactly what the format string says. Without \n, each call's output abuts the next, producing one run-on line.
commonMistakes: Expecting Printf to add a newline like Println does.
Forgetting the \n at the end of a Printf format string.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add a newline to the format string so each item is on its own line.

theory.question: What is the difference between fmt.Println, fmt.Printf, and fmt.Sprintf?
theory.directAnswer: Println writes its operands separated by spaces and adds a trailing newline. Printf writes according to a format string with verbs and adds nothing extra — you include \n yourself. Sprintf is like Printf but returns the formatted string instead of writing it to standard output.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three output functions differing in formatting control and destination.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To cover quick printing (Println), controlled formatting (Printf), and string building (Sprintf).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Println auto-spaces and newlines; Printf/Sprintf interpret verbs; the S-prefix returns a string rather than writing.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the right one avoids run-on output and unnecessary string allocations — basic but commonly muddled.
theory.realWorldExample: Build a log message with Sprintf, then pass it to a logger; use Printf for ad-hoc console formatting.

followUps.question: What's the difference between Print and Println?
followUps.answer: Print adds spaces only between non-string operands and no trailing newline; Println always spaces operands and appends a newline.

followUps.question: How do you write formatted output to a file?
followUps.answer: Use fmt.Fprintf(w, format, args...) where w is any io.Writer such as an *os.File.

theory.question: What is the Stringer interface and when would you implement it?
theory.directAnswer: fmt.Stringer is interface { String() string }. If a type implements it, fmt functions use String() to format the value for %v and %s. Implement it to give your type a clean, human-readable textual form in logs and output instead of the default field dump.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A one-method interface that lets a type define its own print representation.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So custom types can present readable output without callers writing formatting code.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: fmt detects Stringer via reflection and calls String() when formatting with %v/%s.

theory.whyImportant: It centralizes formatting and improves log readability — a common idiomatic-Go question.
theory.realWorldExample: A Status enum implements String() so it logs as 'ACTIVE' instead of the underlying integer.

followUps.question: What's the risk of calling fmt inside String()?
followUps.answer: If String() formats the same value with %v, it can recurse infinitely; format the underlying fields, not the type itself.

followUps.question: Does error relate to Stringer?
followUps.answer: error's Error() string is analogous; fmt prefers Error() over String() when both exist for the %v/%s of an error value.

theory.question: What is the difference between the %v, %+v, and %#v verbs?
theory.directAnswer: %v prints a value's default representation (for a struct, just the field values like {1 Ann}). %+v adds the struct field names ({ID:1 Name:Ann}). %#v prints the Go-syntax representation — the literal you could paste back into code, including the type name (main.User{ID:1, Name:"Ann"}).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three general-purpose formatting verbs that render any value with progressively more detail.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To give developers a spectrum from compact output (%v) to fully self-describing, copy-pasteable output (%#v) for debugging.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: fmt uses reflection to inspect the operand's type. %v walks fields printing values; %+v also emits field names; %#v emits the type name and a Go literal with quoted strings.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the right verb turns an opaque debug dump into a readable one — a very common day-to-day and interview distinction.
theory.realWorldExample: When logging a request config struct during debugging, %+v shows which field held an unexpected value without you counting positions.

followUps.question: How does %v format a value that implements Stringer?
followUps.answer: It calls the type's String() method, so %v yields the custom textual form rather than the default field dump.

followUps.question: Why might %#v be preferred in test failure messages?
followUps.answer: Because it emits an unambiguous, type-annotated Go literal, making it clear exactly what value was produced (including string quoting and nil-vs-empty distinctions).

theory.question: Why should you never pass untrusted or dynamic input as the format string to Printf?
theory.directAnswer: The first argument to Printf is a format string interpreted for verbs like %d and %s. If untrusted input contains % sequences, fmt tries to interpret them as verbs, producing garbled output or bad-verb errors like %!s(MISSING), and it leaks nothing useful. The safe pattern is fmt.Printf("%s", userInput) or fmt.Print(userInput), passing the input as an operand, not as the format string.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A format-string safety issue where user data is mistakenly used as the template rather than as data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Printf's first parameter is always parsed for verbs; it cannot tell that the caller meant the % signs literally.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Passing input as an operand with a fixed "%s" format string means fmt only substitutes it once, treating any % characters inside as literal text.

theory.whyImportant: It prevents corrupted logs and confusing output, and go vet flags the mistake (Printf-family checks) in code review.
theory.realWorldExample: Logging a user-supplied filename directly as fmt.Printf(name) breaks when someone uploads a file named report-50%done.txt; fmt.Printf("%s", name) prints it correctly.

followUps.question: How does go vet help here?
followUps.answer: vet's printf analyzer warns when a non-constant format string is used or when operands don't match verbs, catching the bug before it ships.

followUps.question: What does %!s(MISSING) mean?
followUps.answer: It is fmt's bad-verb marker indicating a verb had no matching operand — a sign the format string and arguments are out of sync.

scenario.question: A high-throughput logging hot path is showing up in CPU profiles, dominated by fmt.Sprintf. How do you reduce the cost?
scenario.directAnswer: fmt uses reflection per call, which is relatively expensive. For hot paths, replace Sprintf with strconv (Itoa, FormatFloat) and a strings.Builder or a pre-sized []byte, or use structured logging that avoids per-line formatting. Reserve fmt for cold paths and human-facing output.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A performance issue from reflection-based formatting in a tight loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: fmt inspects each operand's type at runtime, adding overhead per call.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: strconv formats known types directly without reflection; a Builder reuses one buffer instead of allocating per Sprintf.

scenario.whyImportant: Logging and formatting are common, easy-to-miss hot spots in throughput-sensitive services.
scenario.realWorldExample: Switching a metrics-emitting loop from Sprintf to strconv.AppendInt on a reused buffer cut its CPU usage substantially.

followUps.question: How would you confirm the win?
followUps.answer: Benchmark with testing.B and -benchmem, and re-profile with pprof to confirm fmt is no longer dominating.

scenario.question: You need an HTTP handler to stream a formatted report directly to the client without building a huge string in memory first. How do you use fmt to do this?
scenario.directAnswer: Write with fmt.Fprintf(w, ...) where w is the http.ResponseWriter, which implements io.Writer. Each Fprintf call writes formatted bytes straight to the response stream, so you never accumulate the whole report in a string. This is the same generalization that lets fmt target files, buffers, or network connections.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Using fmt's Fprintf family to send formatted output to an arbitrary io.Writer destination rather than to a string or stdout.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So formatting logic is decoupled from the destination — any type with a Write([]byte) method can receive fmt output.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: http.ResponseWriter satisfies io.Writer; Fprintf formats each line and calls Write, streaming bytes to the client incrementally instead of allocating one large Sprintf result.

scenario.whyImportant: Streaming avoids large memory spikes for big responses and is the idiomatic way fmt integrates with the net/http and io ecosystems.
scenario.realWorldExample: A CSV export endpoint loops over database rows calling fmt.Fprintf(w, "%d,%q\n", id, name), flushing rows to the browser as they are read.

followUps.question: What error handling does Fprintf offer that Printf makes easy to ignore?
followUps.answer: Fprintf returns the byte count and an error; on a network writer that error matters (e.g., client disconnect), whereas Printf's error to stdout is usually ignored.

followUps.question: Would you still reach for strconv here?
followUps.answer: Only if the loop is extremely hot; for typical export sizes Fprintf's clarity outweighs the reflection cost, but a profile could justify strconv.AppendInt into a buffer.

systemDesign.question: Design a consistent, testable output-formatting layer for a CLI tool that must support both human-readable and machine-parseable (JSON) output.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Introduce an abstraction that writes to an io.Writer rather than to stdout directly, so output is testable with a bytes.Buffer. Define a Renderer interface (e.g., Render(w io.Writer, data any) error) with two implementations: a text renderer that uses fmt.Fprintf and the Stringer interface on your types, and a JSON renderer using encoding/json. Select the implementation from a --format flag. Keep fmt for the human path and never build format strings from user data.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered design separating what to output (data) from how (format) and where (destination), built on io.Writer and fmt.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: CLIs commonly need friendly output for humans and structured output for pipelines; hard-coding fmt.Printf everywhere makes both testing and adding formats painful.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Business logic returns typed values; a Renderer chosen at startup writes them to an injected io.Writer. The text Renderer leans on Stringer/%+v for readable lines; the JSON Renderer marshals the same values. Tests pass a bytes.Buffer and assert on its contents.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It makes output uniform, unit-testable (no capturing os.Stdout), and extensible to new formats without touching core logic.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: kubectl-style tools implement exactly this: a shared command produces objects, and -o wide/json/yaml selects a renderer that writes to the command's output stream.

followUps.question: Why inject io.Writer instead of calling fmt.Println directly?
followUps.answer: Injection lets tests capture output in a buffer and lets the same code target files, pipes, or the response writer without change.

followUps.question: Where does Stringer fit in this design?
followUps.answer: In the text renderer: giving domain types a String() method centralizes their human format so every %v/%s prints them consistently.

followUps.question: How do you keep the two renderers in sync?
followUps.answer: Have both consume the same typed data structures, and add golden-file tests per format so a field change surfaces in both outputs.

coding.question: Implement `func Table(rows [][]string) string` that formats a 2D slice of strings into a left-aligned, column-padded text table.
coding.thoughtProcess: First compute each column's max width, then use fmt.Sprintf with a dynamic width verb (%-*s for left-align to a width) to pad each cell. Build the output with a strings.Builder to avoid repeated allocations, adding a newline after each row.
coding.lineByLine: We size widths to the column count and scan every cell to find the widest entry per column. Then we use fmt.Fprintf into a strings.Builder with %-*s, where * takes the width argument and - left-aligns, padding each cell to its column width. A trailing newline ends each row, and Builder.String returns the assembled table cheaply.

followUps.question: What does the * in %-*s do?
followUps.answer: It takes the field width from an argument (the next operand) instead of hard-coding it, enabling dynamic column widths.

followUps.question: Why Fprintf into a Builder instead of Sprintf + concatenation?
followUps.answer: Builder grows one buffer, avoiding the O(n^2) allocations of repeated string concatenation.

coding.question: Implement a Duration type (based on int seconds) whose String() method makes it print as "HH:MM:SS" whenever it is formatted with %v or %s.
coding.thoughtProcess: The fmt package calls a value's String() method for %v and %s if the type satisfies fmt.Stringer (String() string). So I define a named type over int and give it a String method. Inside, I split total seconds into hours, minutes, and seconds with integer division and modulo, then format them zero-padded to two digits each using fmt.Sprintf with the %02d verb.
coding.lineByLine: Duration is a named type over int so we can attach a method. String computes hours via total/3600, minutes via (total%3600)/60, and seconds via total%60. fmt.Sprintf with %02d zero-pads each component to two digits. Because the type implements fmt.Stringer, fmt.Printf("%v", d) and fmt.Println(d) automatically invoke String() and print 01:01:01 for 3661 seconds.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a fixed number of arithmetic and formatting operations.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a small fixed-length output string.

followUps.question: Should String() be defined on the value or pointer receiver here?
followUps.answer: A value receiver is best for a small int-based type: it lets both Duration and *Duration satisfy Stringer, so %v works whether you pass the value or a pointer.

followUps.question: How could String() accidentally recurse?
followUps.answer: If it formatted the receiver itself with %v (e.g., fmt.Sprintf("%v", d)), fmt would call String() again forever; formatting the underlying int fields avoids this.

keyTakeaways: fmt provides Print/Println/Printf for output and Sprintf for building strings; Println auto-spaces and newlines, Printf does exactly what its verbs say.
Know the core verbs: %d (int), %s (string), %f (float), %t (bool), %v (default), %+v (field names), %#v (Go syntax), %q (quoted).
Implement String() (fmt.Stringer) to control how your types print, and use Fprintf to write formatted output to any io.Writer.
fmt uses reflection, so it's flexible but slower in hot paths — reach for strconv and a strings.Builder there, and never pass untrusted input as the format string.
